questions.q: How is the photoelectric effect defined?
options: The release of electrons from a metal surface exposed to electromagnetic radiation
The heating of a metal surface until it glows and emits light
The reflection of ultraviolet light from a clean metal surface
The continuous flow of charge through a metal when a voltage is applied
questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect is the name given to the release of electrons from a metal surface exposed to electromagnetic radiation; for example, when a clean surface of sodium metal is exposed to ultraviolet light, electrons are liberated from the surface. The ejected electrons are called photoelectrons.

questions.q: In Hallwachs' experiment a clean zinc plate is attached to a gold leaf electroscope. What is observed when ultraviolet light from an arc lamp shines on the zinc?
options: A positively charged electroscope discharges quickly, but a negatively charged one is unaffected
A negatively charged electroscope discharges quickly, but a positively charged one shows no fast discharge
Both positively and negatively charged electroscopes discharge at the same rate
The electroscope gains charge regardless of its initial sign
questions.explanation: Hallwachs charged the electroscope negatively and the charge leaked away quickly when the zinc was exposed to ultraviolet light, because the light ejects electrons. If the electroscope was positively charged there was no fast discharge, since any ejected electron is pulled straight back.

questions.q: What did J.J. Thomson establish in 1899 about the particles emitted from zinc by ultraviolet light?
options: That they were positively charged ions liberated from the metal
That they were the same particles, electrons, that are found in cathode rays
That they were photons carrying the energy of the light
That they were emitted only when a strong electric field was applied
questions.explanation: In 1899 J.J. Thomson established that the ultraviolet light caused electrons to be emitted from a sheet of zinc metal and showed that these electrons were the same particles found in cathode rays. The new feature was that the electrons were ejected by radiation rather than by a strong electric field.

questions.q: In Lenard's apparatus the collector is charged negatively to repel the photoelectrons. What is the stopping voltage?
options: The voltage that accelerates the photoelectrons towards the collector
The value of the voltage at which the photocurrent drops to zero
The voltage produced by a single photoelectron striking the collector
The voltage at which the photocurrent first begins to flow
questions.explanation: The voltage is applied across the variable resistor to oppose the motion of the photoelectrons, and the value of the voltage at which the current drops to zero is known as the stopping voltage. For a given frequency the photoelectrons are emitted with the same maximum kinetic energy, because the electrons are all stopped by the same voltage.

questions.q: From memory, state the three things Lenard observed when he varied the intensity and frequency of the light striking the metal.
keyPoints: Doubling the light intensity would double the number of electrons emitted (so the photocurrent increases with intensity).
There was no change in the kinetic energy of the photoelectrons as the light intensity increased.
The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on the frequency of the light illuminating the metal.
questions.explanation: Lenard filtered the arc light to investigate different frequencies. He found intensity controls the number of electrons, while the maximum kinetic energy is set by frequency, not intensity. If you recalled all three, grade it Good or Easy.

questions.q: Electrons are emitted from a metal surface with a maximum kinetic energy of 2.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the stopping voltage that will just reduce the photocurrent to zero. (Charge on an electron = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
questions.explanation: The stopping voltage relates to the maximum kinetic energy by \(E_k = qV_0\), so \(V_0 = E_k / q\). Joules divided by coulombs gives volts; a stopping voltage of 1.6 V will stop the electrons emitted from the surface.

questions.q: A stopping voltage of 4.2 V is required to reduce the photocurrent to zero. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (Charge on an electron = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.)
questions.explanation: Rearranging the stopping-voltage relationship \(E_k = qV_0\) the other way, a 4.2 V stopping voltage will stop electrons with energy 6.7 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. This is the maximum kinetic energy, since the stopping voltage turns back even the fastest electron.

questions.q: There exists a threshold frequency below which the photoelectric effect does not occur, independent of intensity. What does the wave model predict about a threshold frequency?
options: A sharp threshold frequency should exist, fixed by the amplitude of the wave
No threshold effect should exist, because energy transfer to the electrons is accumulative and emission will eventually occur
The threshold frequency should rise as the intensity of the light increases
Emission should occur only at one exact frequency and nowhere else
questions.explanation: The wave model predicts no threshold effect should exist, as energy transfer to electrons from the light source is accumulative and eventually emission will occur. This contradicts the observed threshold frequency, which is independent of intensity, so the wave model fails.

questions.q: From memory, recall the DENF memory hook for the four observations of the photoelectric effect.
keyPoints: D — no Delay: electrons are emitted essentially instantly, even when the light is very faint.
E — Energy from frequency: the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends only on the frequency (colour), not the intensity.
N — Number from intensity: brightness controls how many electrons come off per second (the photocurrent), not their energy.
F — threshold Frequency: below a cut-off frequency no electrons are emitted, no matter how intense or prolonged the light.
questions.explanation: DENF is the carry-the-rest-of-the-course hook: no Delay, Energy from frequency, Number from intensity, threshold Frequency. Of these four, the wave model gets three wrong and only Number-from-intensity right.

questions.q: Explain how the observations of the photoelectric effect provide evidence against the wave model of light. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: According to the wave model, light is a continuous wave whose energy depends on its intensity and is spread continuously over the metal surface. This model makes predictions that three of the four photoelectric observations contradict. First, the wave model predicts that with faint light an electron would need time to absorb enough energy to escape, so there should be a time delay before emission; however, electrons are emitted almost instantaneously even for very faint light. Second, the wave model predicts that light of any frequency should eventually eject electrons if it is intense enough; however, there is a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted, no matter how intense the light or how long it shines. Third, the wave model predicts that the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons should increase with the intensity of the light; however, the maximum kinetic energy depends only on the frequency and is independent of intensity. The only observation consistent with the wave model is that increasing the intensity increases the number of photoelectrons per second. Since three of the four key observations directly contradict the predictions of the wave model, the photoelectric effect provides strong evidence that the wave model of light is incomplete.

criteria.descriptor: States the wave model's basis: continuous wave whose energy depends on intensity, spread across the surface.
Pairs the no-delay observation with the wave prediction of a time delay for faint light.
Pairs the threshold frequency with the wave prediction that any frequency should work if intense enough.
Pairs energy-from-frequency with the wave prediction that energy should rise with intensity.
Acknowledges the one observation the wave model gets right: number of electrons rises with intensity.
Concludes that, with three of four observations contradicted, the wave model is incomplete.

questions.explanation: The marks live in the contrast: for each failure pair the wave-model prediction with the contradicting observation (prediction X, observation Y), then finish with a judgement. Listing the observations alone earns roughly half marks. Note this answer never mentions photons — that is Part 2.
